Your bond matures in ten years, but the bill arrives in three: chart the timing mismatch

Use four graphics to separate fixed coupon payments, changing bond prices and the cash available when a goal arrives before or after maturity.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Original annual-coupon, non-callable bullet-bond illustration in nominal CAD. Purchase is immediately after a coupon date with no accrued interest. The selected reset yield applies immediately after purchase and stays constant. Each annual coupon is paid in full; maturity principal is paid in full. Goal-date values are immediately after that year’s coupon or maturity payment. Coupons and matured principal are held as zero-interest cash, with no reinvestment. Price is the present value of remaining annual coupons and face at the selected effective annual yield. No issuer default, credit-spread change, bid-ask spread, dealing costs, taxes, currency movement, optionality, amortization or product quotation is modeled. Assuming timely payment is not a guarantee. Yield to maturity is a discount rate here, not the realized return with idle coupon cash.

The central idea

A fixed coupon does not fix the amount you can receive from an early sale. Match the investment’s cash dates to the date of the spending goal.

01

Separate face amount, purchase price and coupon

A bond can carry a fixed coupon and still have a changing market price. The face amount is the principal the issuer is scheduled to repay at maturity. The purchase price is what the buyer pays today. The coupon is a contractual cash payment, often expressed as a percentage of face. These quantities are related but are not interchangeable.

In the default illustration, CAD 10,000 of face pays a CAD 400 annual coupon for ten years. At a 4% effective annual discount yield, its price immediately after a coupon date is CAD 10,000. Changing the market yield does not rewrite that CAD 400 coupon in this fixed-coupon example; it changes what a buyer would pay for the remaining payments.

The SEC’s investor bulletin on interest-rate risk explains the general relationship between fixed-rate bond prices and market rates. Our chart supplies a separate annual-payment calculation. It is not a current bond offer or an estimate of a particular issuer’s creditworthiness.

02

A scheduled principal repayment may arrive after your bill

If the cash goal is three years away and the bond matures in ten, funding the goal from the bond can require a sale with seven years still outstanding. The scheduled maturity principal does not automatically become available at year three. The sale price depends on the remaining cash flows and the yield a buyer requires at that time.

The tool applies the selected yield reset immediately after purchase and keeps that yield constant afterward. At a reset to 6%, the default bond is worth about CAD 8,528 immediately after the change. Its later market value moves toward maturity value as the remaining term shortens, assuming all payments occur as modeled.

This is a controlled pricing scenario, not a forecast of an interest-rate path. Actual market prices also respond to changing credit spreads, trading conditions, optionality and other factors omitted here. An issuer failing to pay would invalidate the assumed coupon and principal receipts.

03

Include the coupon cash exactly once

The path chart adds three possible components: the current market value of a still-outstanding bond, coupons already received and retained, and principal received at maturity. Before maturity, retained principal is zero. After maturity, the outstanding bond value is zero. This prevents counting the principal twice.

Coupons and maturity proceeds earn no interest in this illustration. At a goal date after maturity, the wealth line is therefore flat once the final coupon and principal have arrived. A personal plan could reinvest that cash, but then it would need a reinvestment rate, payment schedule and another risk assessment.

The chart’s points fall immediately after each annual coupon or maturity payment. The purchase occurs immediately after a coupon boundary with no accrued interest. Real bonds often pay on a different schedule, and an actual settlement can include accrued interest and dealing costs.

04

Read the present-value formula behind the price

For face amount F, annual coupon C, effective annual yield y and N remaining annual payments, the price is the sum of C ÷ (1 + y)t for t = 1 to N, plus F ÷ (1 + y)N. A higher discount yield reduces the present value of those same promised amounts.

At zero yield, price becomes F + NC. At the coupon rate, an ordinary annual-coupon bond at a coupon boundary prices at face in this simplified model. These are useful mathematical checks, not evidence that a particular instrument is offered at those levels.

The matrix changes term and yield while preserving face and coupon. A cell is a price at one date. It does not include coupons already received or a future return calculation. Compare the same column across terms to see how a longer stream of fixed payments changes the sensitivity.

05

A holding-period dollar gain is different from the quoted yield

The waterfall adds retained coupons to exit value or maturity principal, then subtracts the original purchase price. The total is a nominal holding-period gain or loss in dollars. A positive coupon step can be offset by selling below the purchase price; coupon income alone does not describe the whole result.

The purchase yield is used to discount the initial cash flows. It is not automatically the realized compound return when coupons sit idle and the bond is sold before maturity. This article deliberately does not label the dollar gain as an annualized yield or calculate an investor’s after-tax result.

For a dated goal, record each usable cash receipt and the amount that depends on an early sale. Compare that calendar with the bill date. A suitable plan also considers the issuer, currency, liquidity, fees, tax treatment and whether other resources can cover a price shortfall. Maturity matching addresses one timing issue; it does not remove every investment risk.
